_note: Witness lists are simplified to the major witnesses the UI displays. Confirm each against NA28 apparatus / SBLGNT apparatus before shipping. 'contains' = true means the witness includes the disputed text.
sources: Nestle-Aland 28 apparatus; SBL Greek New Testament apparatus (open)
Bruce Metzger, A Textual Commentary on the Greek New Testament, 2nd ed.
Daniel Wallace on variant categories (CSNTM lectures/essays)

passages.title: The angel who stirred the water
passages.disputed_text: ...waiting for the moving of the water; for an angel went down at certain seasons into the pool and stirred the water; whoever stepped in first after the stirring was healed of whatever disease he had.
passages.context_before: In these lay a multitude of invalids, blind, lame, paralyzed
passages.context_after: One man was there who had been an invalid for thirty-eight years.
passages.explanation: Verse 7 has the man say the water is 'stirred up' with no prior explanation. A marginal gloss explaining the local belief was absorbed into the text in some copies by the 4th-5th century. The earliest witnesses lack it.
passages.doctrine_impact: None. Huff's own example: the verse number is retained and the text is in your footnote.

passages.title: The longer ending of Mark
passages.disputed_text: Now when he rose early on the first day of the week, he appeared first to Mary Magdalene... (twelve verses)
passages.context_before: ...and they said nothing to anyone, for they were afraid.
passages.explanation: Sinaiticus and Vaticanus end at 16:8; several later manuscripts mark the ending as doubtful. Vocabulary and style differ from the rest of Mark. Almost all modern Bibles print it with brackets and a note.
passages.doctrine_impact: No doctrine rests on it alone; snake-handling and poison-drinking sects have leaned on 16:18.

passages.title: The woman caught in adultery
passages.disputed_text: ...Let him who is without sin among you be the first to throw a stone at her...
passages.explanation: Absent from every early Greek witness; appears in Bezae (5th c.) and later, and floats to other locations (after Luke 21:38 in some). Likely an authentic early tradition about Jesus that was not originally part of John.
passages.doctrine_impact: None; the story's ethic is consistent with the rest of the Gospels.

passages.title: The Johannine Comma
passages.disputed_text: ...in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Holy Spirit; and these three are one. And there are three that bear witness on earth...
passages.context_before: For there are three that testify:
passages.context_after: the Spirit and the water and the blood; and these three agree.
passages.explanation: Found in no Greek manuscript before the 14th century; entered Erasmus's 3rd edition (1522) from a Latin tradition, and from there the KJV. Every modern translation omits it.
passages.doctrine_impact: The Trinity is argued from many other passages; no modern theologian rests it on this verse.

passages.title: The angel and the bloody sweat
passages.disputed_text: And there appeared to him an angel from heaven, strengthening him. And being in agony he prayed more earnestly; and his sweat became like great drops of blood falling down to the ground.
passages.explanation: Early and geographically wide support on both sides. Modern editions bracket it. Ehrman argues it was added against docetism; others argue it was removed for the same reason.

passages.title: The doxology of the Lord's Prayer
passages.disputed_text: For yours is the kingdom and the power and the glory, forever. Amen.
passages.context_after: For if you forgive others their trespasses...
passages.explanation: A liturgical ending (cf. 1 Chronicles 29:11) that entered the text through use in worship. Absent from the earliest witnesses and from Luke's version.

passages.title: One letter: 'we have' vs 'let us have'
passages.disputed_text: ἔχομεν (we have peace) vs ἔχωμεν (let us have peace)
passages.context_before: Therefore, since we have been justified by faith,
passages.context_after: ...peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ.
passages.explanation: Omicron and omega were pronounced alike; scribes writing from dictation confused them constantly. Even here, where the better manuscripts read 'let us have', editors print 'we have' on internal grounds.

passages.title: 'Only Son' vs 'only God'
passages.disputed_text: μονογενὴς θεός (only God) vs μονογενὴς υἱός (only Son)
passages.context_before: No one has ever seen God;
passages.context_after: ...who is at the Father's side, he has made him known.
passages.explanation: Both nouns were abbreviated as two-letter nomina sacra (ΘΣ / ΥΣ), one stroke apart. The earliest papyri read 'God'; the majority read 'Son'.
passages.doctrine_impact: Either reading affirms Christ's divinity in John's context; the difference is which word John used to say it.

categories._note: Approximate shares of the ~400,000 total variants, per Wallace's popular taxonomy. Present as estimates.
